results.content:
Mouse is introducing Mouse-1, a general-purpose decision model built for AI agent harnesses, as described in mouse.dev's report. It integrates into an existing harness through a single API and returns a decision in about 100 milliseconds of model time. Mouse designed it so agents complete more work independently, with fewer errors and fewer unnecessary interruptions. In Mouse's tests, Mouse-1 was 163× faster than GPT-6 Sol and returned a decision before Sol produced its first token.

This piece covers the accuracy tables, the scoring call, image input, tuning, and the cost of 1,000 decisions. It is for engineers who already run an agent harness and want a separate model to score options while a larger model plans and writes code. [...] ## Mouse-1 – a decision model for your agent: why it matters now

Agents make many decisions as they operate. Mouse says those decisions compound over time and are becoming more important as agents work for hours and even days at a time. Mouse built Mouse-1 as a common interface for those choices and says adding it to Mouse's own coding agent harness significantly improves latency. The posted speed mark remains 163× versus GPT-6 Sol at about 100 ms of model time. Separately, Mouse prices the model at up to 65× cheaper than frontier models per 1,000 decisions. results.title: Why Your Agent Harness Needs a Decision Model | prompt2bot
results.content:
## 1. Dynamic Skill Hydration

A common failure mode in production agents is prompt bloat. Developers want their bot to handle coding, calendar management, database querying, and document retrieval. The easiest approach is to load every skill, prompt guideline, and tool schema into the system prompt at the start of every turn.

This poisons model attention. When a model has forty tools and fifteen pages of instructions in its context, tool selection accuracy drops and latency spikes.

Instead of stuffing the prompt upfront, our harness uses a decision model to evaluate candidate skills against the conversation state. For every available skill, the decision model answers a simple truth question: does the current turn or user request require this capability? [...] ## What is a Decision Model?

A decision model does not generate freeform token streams. Instead, it evaluates a state against a bounded hypothesis space.

Within the harness, there are multiple places where decisions are made about how to use the LLM: which skills to load into context, whether to compact past logs, which model tier to route to, or whether a response is grounded enough to send.

Most of these control points do not need open-ended generation. They evaluate runtime state through a few discrete decision shapes: [...] The discrete fields are evaluated via the decision model.
 The generative text fields are handled by a generative model call.

Both run concurrently using `Promise.all`, and the harness stitches the validated result back into a single typed object. The decision model handles the classification deterministically, while the generative model focuses purely on synthesizing natural language.

## Decouple Deciding from Generating

Generative models are great at synthesizing language, explaining nuanced concepts, and writing code. They are surprisingly poor choices for the deterministic plumbing of an agent harness.
